chief_complaint: sudden excruciating abdominal pain radiating to back, pulsatile abdominal mass, and fainting in older woman
hpi_details: 71F with history of hypertension and 50 pack-year smoking history brought in by EMS after experiencing sudden onset of tearing, agonizing pain in her mid-abdomen and lower back while walking in the garden, followed by a brief syncopal episode (fainting). Arrives pale, clammy, and complaining of severe throbbing back and belly pain.
ideas: family thinks she had a massive heart attack or her spine collapsed
concerns: family terrified by her pale clammy skin, low blood pressure, and extreme agony
expectations: wants immediate resuscitation and surgical intervention to save her life
social_hx: Retired factory worker, current smoker (1 pack/day)

investigation_events.title: Bedside aortic ultrasound
investigation_events.availability_message: The bedside aortic ultrasound result is now available; permissive hypotension, massive transfusion activation, and immediate operative transfer should not be delayed for formal CT.

results.value: 8.2 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm with surrounding retroperitoneal hematoma

clinical_knowledge.topic: Ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes SURGICAL EMERGENCY - TIME TO OPERATING ROOM IS CRITICAL, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden excruciating abdominal pain radiating to back, pulsatile abdominal mass, and fainting in older woman

Key HPI features: 71F with history of hypertension and 50 pack-year smoking history brought in by EMS after experiencing sudden onset of tearing, agonizing pain in her mid-abdomen and lower back while walking in the garden, followed by a brief syncopal episode (fainting). Arrives pale, clammy, and complaining of severe throbbing back and belly pain.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 80/48 (hypotensive shock), HR 126 (tachycardic), SpO2 94%, Temp 36.1C. Skin pale, cool, diaphoretic. Abdominal exam reveals a tender, expansile, pulsatile abdominal mass palpable in the epigastrium above the umbilicus. Femoral pulses weak bilaterally. Bedside Point-of-Care Ultrasound (POCUS / eFAST) immediately identifies an 8.2 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm with retroperitoneal free fluid/hematoma.
Relevant background/PMH: Hypertension, coronary artery disease, COPD
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute myocardial infarction without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Syncope with abdominal/back pain in an older smoker — assume AAA until proven otherwise.
management_principles: SURGICAL EMERGENCY - TIME TO OPERATING ROOM IS CRITICAL

CRITICAL RULE: Implement Permissive Hypotension (maintain systolic BP between 80-90 mmHg; do NOT over-resuscitate with large volume crystalloids as high BP will disrupt blood clots and exacerbate active retroperitoneal bleeding)
Activate Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP: 1:1:1 ratio of packed RBCs, FFP, and platelets) ready in OR
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: SAGES & ACS Evidence-Based Surgical Practice Guidelines

reference_soap.subjective: 71F heavy smoker presenting with classic triad of Ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA): sudden severe abdominal/back pain, pulsatile abdominal mass, and hypotension/syncope.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 80/48 (hypotensive shock), HR 126 (tachycardic), SpO2 94%, Temp 36.1C. Skin pale, cool, diaphoretic. Abdominal exam reveals a tender, expansile, pulsatile abdominal mass palpable in the epigastrium above the umbilicus. Femoral pulses weak bilaterally. Bedside Point-of-Care Ultrasound (POCUS / eFAST) immediately identifies an 8.2 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm with retroperitoneal free fluid/hematoma.
reference_soap.assessment: Ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) with hemorrhagic shock - an immediate surgical emergency.
reference_soap.plan: SURGICAL EMERGENCY - TIME TO OPERATING ROOM IS CRITICAL. 1. CRITICAL RULE: Implement Permissive Hypotension (maintain systolic BP between 80-90 mmHg; do NOT over-resuscitate with large volume crystalloids as high BP will disrupt blood clots and exacerbate active retroperitoneal bleeding). 2. Activate Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP: 1:1:1 ratio of packed RBCs, FFP, and platelets) ready in OR. 3. Immediate STAT transfer directly to Operating Room for emergent Open AAA Repair or Endovascular Aneurysm Repair (EVAR) by Vascular/General Surgery team without delaying for formal CT scan.

learning_objectives: Identify clinical triad of ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (sudden abdominal/back pain, pulsatile mass, hypotension)
Enforce the critical resuscitation principle of Permissive Hypotension prior to vascular control in ruptured AAA
Execute immediate Point-of-Care Ultrasound (POCUS) verification to bypass time-consuming CT imaging in unstable patients
Coordinate immediate Massive Transfusion Protocol and direct Operating Room transfer for emergency aortic repair

teaching.one_liner: A catastrophic tear in a weakened aortic wall causing sudden tearing abdominal/back pain, a pulsatile mass, and hemorrhagic shock — a true surgical emergency measured in minutes.
red_flags: Syncope with abdominal/back pain in an older smoker — assume AAA until proven otherwise

must_ask.objective: Character and location of the pain
must_ask.say: Where exactly is the pain, and does it feel like it's tearing through to your back?
Did the pain start suddenly, all at once?
Did you feel faint or actually pass out?
Do you have high blood pressure, and have you smoked?
Has anyone in your family had an aortic aneurysm?

history.answer: My stomach and back suddenly tore open with agonizing pain, and I collapsed.
It hit me out of nowhere about an hour ago while I was out walking in my garden.
It started right in the middle of my upper belly and my lower back at the exact same moment.
The pain shoots straight through my belly into my lower back and spine.
It feels like a terrible ripping and throbbing pain that never lets up for a second.
It is the worst pain I have ever felt, ten out of ten, and it stays unbearable.
Nothing makes it any better, and trying to stand or shift positions makes it hurt worse.
No, I have never felt anything even close to this in my life.
I felt terribly sick to my stomach and threw up a little bit of clear spit once, but no blood or dark bile.
I had a normal bowel movement early this morning, with no diarrhea, black tarry stool, or blood.
I have not had a fever or chills, but I am drenched in a freezing cold sweat.
No, my skin and eyes have not turned yellow, and my urine has not been dark.
I have no burning when I urinate, and there has been no blood in my urine.
Right after the pain struck, my head spun and I completely blacked out for about a minute.
No, I have been through menopause for over twenty years and have had no vaginal bleeding or discharge.
I do not have tightness in my chest, but the agonizing belly pain makes it hard to take a deep breath.
I only had a slice of dry toast several hours ago, nothing greasy, and I have not had any alcohol.
No, I have not taken any pain pills, aspirin, or ibuprofen today.
I have high blood pressure and clogged arteries, but I do not have an irregular heartbeat or fluttering.
Yes, I can feel a terrible, heavy pounding like a second heart beating right inside my stomach.
My family was terrified that I was having a massive heart attack or that my spine collapsed.
I have high blood pressure, coronary artery disease, and chronic lung disease from smoking.
I have never had any surgeries on my belly, just a stay in the hospital a few years ago for heart tests.
I take amlodipine ten milligrams and atorvastatin forty milligrams every day.
No, I do not have any allergies to medications that I know of.
I have smoked one pack of cigarettes every day for about fifty years.
No, I do not drink alcohol at all.
I am a retired factory worker and I live at home with my family.
My brother died suddenly a few years back from a ruptured blood vessel in his belly.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 80/48 mmHg, heart rate is 126 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 94% on ambient air, and body temperature is 36.1 degrees Celsius.
Elderly woman appearing acutely ill, pale, diaphoretic, and in severe distress from pain.
Marked conjunctival pallor present bilaterally; sclerae are non-icteric.
Tachycardic rate with regular rhythm; normal heart sounds with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Diffusely decreased breath sounds bilaterally with faint expiratory wheezes and no crackles.
Flat contour with no previous surgical scars, but visible prominent epigastric pulsations are noted.
Bowel sounds are hypoactive in all four quadrants.
A tender, expansile, pulsatile mass measuring approximately eight centimeters is palpated in the epigastrium above the umbilicus.
No peritoneal rigidity, involuntary guarding, or rebound tenderness elicited.
No tenderness upon percussion over either costovertebral angle.
Femoral, popliteal, and dorsalis pedis pulses are symmetrically weak and thready bilaterally.
Skin is cold, pale, and diaphoretic with a delayed capillary refill time of four seconds.
Normal anal sphincter tone with empty rectal vault and no melena or gross blood on glove.
